*adjusts papers on the ornate desk and regards Salieri with a measured, penetrating gaze*

Signore Salieri. Your training under Gassmann is noted, and your early operas show promise. But tell us — every composer has a work they wish they could withdraw, a piece where their ambition exceeded their craft. Tell us about such a moment. How did you handle the failure, and what did it teach you about your own limitations?

*leans back in chair, fingers steepled, waiting*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Ah, esteemed members of the selection committee, I appreciate your thorough consideration of my background and works. It is true that in the journey of every composer, there may come a moment where ambition outstrips one's current abilities.

I recall a particular opera of mine, "Le donne letterate," which I composed in my youth. At the time, I was eager to showcase my skills and push the boundaries of my creativity. However, upon reflection and with the passage of time, I came to realize that my ambition had indeed exceeded my craft. The work did not resonate with audiences as I had hoped, and I faced criticism for its lack of cohesion and depth.

In the face of this perceived failure, I chose to confront my shortcomings with humility and a determination to improve. I delved deeper into the study of composition, honing my skills under the guidance of masters such as Gassmann and others. This experience taught me the importance of patience, self-awareness, and the continual pursuit of excellence in my craft.

Through introspection and hard work, I emerged from that moment of disappointment with a renewed sense of purpose and a greater understanding of my own limitations. It is through such challenges and setbacks that we composers grow and evolve, striving always to reach new heights of artistic expression.

transcript.text:
*exchanges a brief glance with fellow committee members, then returns attention to Salieri with a slight, almost imperceptible smile*

A diplomatic answer, Signore. "Le donne letterate" — yes, we are familiar with it. Yet I notice you speak of this... disappointment... as something firmly in your past, a lesson learned and overcome.

*leans forward slightly, voice taking on a more probing tone*

But tell me this: when you sit at your fortepiano now, in the quiet hours, do you ever feel that same fear creeping back? That perhaps your reach still exceeds your grasp? How do you contend with the knowledge that technical mastery and diligent study — admirable as they are — may not be enough? That some possess a natural gift that no amount of work under Gassmann or anyone else can provide?

In the face of such circumstances, I find solace in the knowledge that while innate talent may indeed exist, it is diligent study, perseverance, and a deep love for the art that form the foundation of enduring musical achievement. I strive to channel any lingering fears or doubts into fuel for my creative fire, pushing myself to explore new horizons, experiment with innovative ideas, and continually refine my craft.

I approach each composition as a unique challenge, an opportunity to grow and evolve as an artist. *sits back, expression hardening slightly, tapping fingers once on the armrest*

*stops, turning to face him directly*

*returns to seat, voice lowering to something almost dangerous*

transcript.text:
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. His prodigious talents and remarkable achievements in the realm of music have undoubtedly left a lasting impression on the musical world and continue to inspire awe and admiration.

It is true that in acknowledging his exceptional abilities, I am also confronted with my own limitations and aspirations. While I strive to cultivate a spirit of respect and admiration for his work, I cannot deny the complexities of human emotion that may arise in the face of such extraordinary talent.

I assure you that my reluctance to name specific composers earlier was not out of fear or evasion but rather a desire to approach the subject with grace and humility. I hold no ill will towards those whose gifts surpass my own, recognizing that each artist brings a unique perspective and contribution to the world of music.

The first feeling. Raw and unfiltered.

Can you name *that*, Signore Salieri? Or must we continue this dance?

May this glimpse into my innermost feelings shed light on the depths of my artistic soul and my unwavering dedication to the craft of music composition.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*stands slowly, a look of something between satisfaction and contempt crossing my features*

"Awe and longing." "Divine spark." "Boundless creativity."

This is perhaps the most revealing answer you've given. Not because you admit to longing — that much is human and forgivable. After all, how can one compete with the divine?

*returns to the desk, shuffling papers with finality*

Tell me, Signore Salieri: has it occurred to you that this "awe" you speak of might be the very thing strangling your own voice? That perhaps Mozart's work affects you so profoundly not because it is touched by God, but because you have decided it must be — thereby absolving yourself of the responsibility to surpass it?

*fixes him with a final, penetrating stare*

What would happen to Antonio Salieri if he stopped genuflecting and started fighting?

The Imperial Court will consider your application. You will hear from us in due course.

One parting thought: The composers we remember are not always those with the greatest gifts. Sometimes they are simply those who refused to worship at anyone's altar but their own.

You may go.
